lessons.title: Selling Property: LTCG Rates, the Indexation Choice and Stamp Duty Value

body.text: For most resident families selling a home bought before 23 July 2024, the tax law now offers a choice: 12.5% on the plain gain, or 20% on an inflation-adjusted gain. You pay whichever is lower, but only if you actually do both calculations.

children.text: Vivek, a 47-year-old consultant in Bengaluru, is selling the Whitefield flat he bought in 2012 for ₹45,00,000. He has a buyer at ₹1,20,00,000. A friend told him the tax would be "12.5% of the profit", which on roughly ₹66,65,000 of gain comes to more than ₹8 lakh. His CA's calculation came to about half that. The difference is the indexation choice.

stats.label: Resident option for pre-23 July 2024 property
stats.context: Pay the lower of the two

children.text: A flat or plot becomes long-term after more than 24 months. Short-term gains are added to your income and taxed at slab rate. Long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% under section 197 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 112 of the 1961 Act), without indexation. For one important group, there is a second route.

markDefs.definition: Adjusting the purchase cost and improvement cost for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index (CII) notified by CBDT each year, so that only the real gain above inflation is taxed.

children.text: If you are a resident individual or resident HUF and you sell land, a building or both that you acquired before 23 July 2024, section 197 caps your tax at the amount you would pay at 20% using
. In practice, you compute tax both ways and pay the lower figure.

body.latex: \text{Indexed Cost} = \text{Cost} \times \frac{\text{CII of year of sale}}{\text{CII of year of acquisition (or 2001-02, if later)}}

body.title: Tax on the Same Sale, Different Purchase Years (Cost ₹48,15,000, Net Sale ₹1,18,80,000)

children.text: The chart shows the pattern. For old purchases, indexation wipes out so much of the gain that the 20% route wins comfortably. For recent purchases, there has been too little inflation for indexation to help, and the 12.5% route is lower. Always run both.

body.title: Who Gets the Choice?
body.question: Each person below sells a flat in tax year 2026-27 after holding it for more than 24 months. Who can choose 20% with indexation?
options: Arun, a non-resident Indian living in Dubai, who bought his Kochi flat in 2015
Neha, a resident, who bought her Pune flat in September 2024
Suresh, a resident, who bought his Chennai flat in 2019
A private limited company selling an office it bought in 2018
body.explanation: The option is only for resident individuals and resident HUFs, and only for land or buildings acquired before 23 July 2024. Arun is a non-resident, Neha bought after 23 July 2024, and a company does not qualify. Only Suresh meets both conditions.

body.title: Index the Cost
body.prompt: Suresh bought his Chennai flat in FY 2019-20 for a total cost of ₹60,00,000, including stamp duty and registration. He sells in FY 2026-27. The CII is 289 for 2019-20 and 384 for 2026-27. What is his indexed cost of acquisition, to the nearest rupee?
body.explanation: Indexed cost = ₹60,00,000 × 384 ÷ 289 = ₹79,72,318. He would deduct this from his net sale value for Method B, then compare 20% of that gain with 12.5% of his plain gain.

body.title: Eligibility for the Indexation Choice
body.textWithBlank: The option to pay 20% with indexation on land or buildings bought before 23 July 2024 is available only to resident individuals and resident ___.
body.explanation: Non-residents, companies, firms and LLPs do not get this choice. They pay 12.5% without indexation on long-term gains from property.

body.title: Ananya Sells Too Soon
body.scenario: Ananya, a resident in the 30% slab, bought a flat in Gurugram in October 2024. A buyer offers her a price in August 2026 that gives her a ₹15,00,000 gain. She has held the flat for 22 months.
body.prompt: What tax would she pay if she sells now, and what if she waits a few months? Does she get the indexation choice?
body.modelAnswer: At 22 months the flat is short-term, so the ₹15,00,000 gain is added to her income and taxed at 30%: ₹4,50,000 before surcharge and cess. If she completes the sale after October 2026, once she has held the flat for more than 24 months, the gain becomes long-term and is taxed at 12.5%: ₹1,87,500. She does not get the indexation choice either way, because she bought after 23 July 2024. Waiting a few months, if the buyer will agree to a later registration date, could save her more than ₹2.5 lakh.

children.text: Two Rules Every Property Seller Meets

Stamp duty value: as Chapter 1, Lesson 3 explained, under section 78 of the 2025 Act (section 50C of the 1961 Act), if the stamp duty value is more than 110% of your agreed price, the stamp duty value becomes your sale value. That higher value then flows into both Method A and Method B.

body.text: TDS by the buyer: when a resident buys property worth ₹50 lakh or more from a resident seller, the buyer must deduct 1% TDS and deposit it. This does not reduce your sale value. It shows up in your Form 26AS and AIS as a credit against your final tax. If you are a non-resident seller, TDS is deducted at much higher rates on the gain, and you may want a lower deduction certificate before the sale.

body.title: Deep Dive: Joint Owners, Inherited Property and Pre-2001 Property

children.text: Joint owners: each co-owner computes their own gain on their share of the sale value and cost, and each decides separately between the two methods if eligible. A husband and wife who each own 50% file two separate computations.

Inherited property: cost is the previous owner's cost. For indexation, courts have generally allowed the CII of the year the previous owner acquired the property, or 2001-02 if later, though the Income Tax Department has at times argued for the year of inheritance. The holding period includes the previous owner's.

Pre-2001 property: you can use fair market value on 1 April 2001 as cost, capped at the stamp duty value on that date, and index it from the CII of 2001-02 (100). Get a registered valuer's report for this.

body.text: The indexation choice only reduces tax. If the indexed computation shows a loss, you should not assume that loss can be set off against other gains or carried forward. Take professional advice when Method B produces a loss.

children.text: A large long-term property gain can often be reduced to zero by reinvesting in another house or in specified bonds. Chapter 5, Lesson 3 covers those exemptions in detail.

cards.definition: Land and buildings become long-term after more than 24 months.
Long-term gain without indexation, taxed at 12.5% under section 197.
For resident individuals and HUFs with property bought before 23 July 2024: 20% on the indexed gain. Pay the lower of A and B.
Cost × CII of year of sale ÷ CII of year of acquisition or 2001-02.
Deducted by the buyer on purchases of ₹50 lakh or more from a resident. A tax credit, not a reduction in sale value.

body.title: Before You Register the Sale Deed
steps: Confirm the holding period is more than 24 months from your purchase registration or allotment date
Collect your purchase deed, stamp duty and registration receipts and improvement bills with dates
Check the stamp duty value of the property against your agreed price and the 110% safe harbour
If you are a resident who bought before 23 July 2024, compute tax both with and without indexation
Ensure the buyer deducts TDS correctly and that it appears in your Form 26AS and AIS
Plan any reinvestment exemption before the sale, since some have strict time limits

points: Property is long-term after more than 24 months; short-term gains are taxed at slab rate
Long-term property gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation under section 197
Resident individuals and HUFs selling property bought before 23 July 2024 pay the lower of 12.5% plain and 20% indexed
Indexation usually wins for older properties, while 12.5% usually wins for recent ones
The stamp duty value can replace your sale price, and buyer TDS is a credit, not a deduction
NRIs, companies and property bought on or after 23 July 2024 get only the 12.5% route

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not tax or investment advice. Property prices, costs and improvement amounts are illustrative. CII values are as notified by CBDT, and sections and rates reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 for tax year 2026-27. Property transactions have many fact-specific issues, so consult a qualified tax professional before selling.
